::: {.why}
It is the most cited model in the field and the most often fitted without anyone stating the claim it makes, which is a specific and testable statement about the persistence of variance.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State what a GARCH(1,1) asserts about tomorrow's variance in one sentence, and what the sum of its two coefficients implies about the long-run variance.
- Say what happens to the model when that sum reaches one, and whether your fit is close to it.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write the recursion out and interpret each term: a constant, a reaction to the last squared shock, and a persistence of the last variance. Then derive the unconditional variance implied by the fit, and say what it means when the coefficient sum exceeds one.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Fit GARCH(1,1), GJR-GARCH and EGARCH with arch on the same series, and report the coefficient estimates, the log-likelihoods and the asymmetry term where present. The asymmetry term is week 6's leverage effect appearing in a model, so check that its sign matches what you measured on day 39.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Compute the implied volatility term structure from your GARCH fit: forecast variance at horizons of 1, 5, 22 and 66 days and plot the path back toward the unconditional level.
:::
:::
